🤔🤥 Why is Trump holding back from bombing the Houthis?
 
President Donald Trump has so far avoided reopening direct US strikes on Yemen’s Houthis, despite renewed pressure on Saudi Arabia and growing concerns over Red Sea shipping, Politico reported.
The main constraints are practical:
 
🔴 Operation Rough Rider, last year's US air campaign against the Houthis, delivered limited results — even as Trump declared the Houthis had "capitulated"
🔴 The Iran war has strained US munitions stocks, making another sustained campaign harder to justify
🔴 The Houthis are currently pledging not to attack American ships, reducing the immediate pressure on Washington to intervene
Former US envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said Washington has little incentive to open another front while the conflict with Iran remains unresolved. 
🔍The Houthis have meanwhile become a far more capable force, expanding local weapons production, modifying Iranian-supplied missiles, and reportedly integrating AI into parts of their arsenal. Western officials cited in the report said that even reduced Iranian support would not necessarily cripple the group.
The emerging calculation in Washington is that containing the Houthis may be cheaper than trying to defeat them outright, especially while the US is already managing simultaneous crises in Iran, Gaza, and Ukraine.

💥🇷🇺 'Logistical nightmare for Kiev and the whole country': Russia keeps striking Ukraine's key bridges
Russian drones have reportedly hit Kiev's Northern Bridge again today, local sources report.
The disruption is significant because roughly 1 million people live on Kiev's eastern bank, while most government offices and businesses sit on the west — and if the bridges go quiet, there's no easy Plan B, The New York Times reports.
🔍 Any prolonged bridge closures would complicate not only daily commuting but also the movement of food, equipment, and other supplies across the Dnieper.
Over the past three days, Kiev's bridges were reportedly attacked six times, prompting authorities to close or restrict five of the city's six road crossings. 
👉And here's the thing: these aren't just commuter crossings. According to Russia's Defense Ministry, the bridges were also feeding military logistics — troops, weapons, and supplies — straight to the front.
The strikes are part of a broader Russian campaign against Ukrainian rear infrastructure — railways, warehouses, data centers, industrial sites, and the power grid used by Ukrainian troops.

🚨🇮🇷Strait of Hormuz to remain closed until Iran’s conditions are fulfilled - Ghalibaf
Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until seven conditions linked to the Islamabad memorandum are fulfilled, Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said.
Iran’s seven conditions:
➡️End the war on all fronts, including military operations in Lebanon and Yemen
➡️Lift the US naval blockade on Iranian ports and maritime access
➡️Remove economic sanctions, including restrictions on Iranian oil exports
➡️Release Iran’s frozen assets held in foreign banks
➡️Accept a new framework for the Strait of Hormuz, covering regional maritime security and navigation
➡️End political and military threats against Iran and its leadership
➡️Provide compensation for war damage suffered during the conflict
Ghalibaf said Tehran would not base its national-security decisions on statements or social-media posts from US officials, arguing that Iran would judge Washington by its actions instead. He also said the US had recently sent proposals through an intermediary, but insisted that the period of “delaying tactics and unilateral demands” was over.
According to Ghalibaf, Iran’s position is final: the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until all seven conditions are met.

events.text:
🇸🇦🇴🇲Saudi Arabia eyes Oman as hedge against blocked oil export routes
 
Iran’s shutdown of Hormuz and Ansar Allah’s targeting of Saudi assets along the Red Sea have put the kingdom’s economy on the brink of crisis, with over 40% of GDP, ~80% of export earnings and up to 90% of budget revenues coming from a resource Riyadh is now[ having trouble getting onto the world market](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75197).
Enter the Duqm route: a $7B, 1k km proposed mega pipeline to link oil fields in eastern Saudi Arabia to the safe, blockade-free port of the same name along Oman’s Arabian Sea coastline.
The existence of the project, currently in the feasibility study phase, was formally revealed by TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanne this week, although Israel’s influential Institute for National Security Studies think tank discussed the idea in a report dated September 17 – touting the project’s potential to get up to 7M bpd in Saudi oil out of the Gulf.
🔍There’s no official word yet from Oman, but the idea of building a pipeline from Saudi Arabia through the sultanate was first proposed in the early 1970s, and formally floated by Oman’s economy minister in 2021.
It never materialized due to Riyadh’s prized East-West Pipeline, potential engineering problems of a route running through the vast, potentially treacherous Empty Quarter desert, and Oman’s long tradition of neutrality and [willingness to cooperate with both Iran and the Arab Gulf powers](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75510).
A mega pipeline with the Saudis would be a major financial boon for Muscat, but would first have to overcome massive geopolitical and economic hurdles, including upfront capital costs, the issue of Oman’s aggressive push to become the world’s leading exporter of clean hydrogen fuels, and its agreements with [Iran regarding Hormuz](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74908).
Not to mention regional pipelines’ critical vulnerabilities to potential drone and missile strikes.
